emergency.ateAvocado.banner.title: Mon chien a mangé un avocat : que faire maintenant
emergency.ateAvocado.banner.subtitle: La chair de l'avocat est légèrement toxique pour les chiens en raison de la persine, mais le noyau est le vrai danger — il peut provoquer une occlusion intestinale mortelle. Appelez votre vétérinaire si le noyau a été avalé.

emergency.ateAvocado.article.ogTitle: Mon chien a mangé un avocat : que faire maintenant | petsMetrics
emergency.ateAvocado.article.ogDescripti: Que faire si votre chien mange de l'avocat.
emergency.ateAvocado.science.content: L'avocat (Persea americana) contient de la persine, un dérivé d'acide gras fongicide. Les chiens sont relativement résistants à la persine comparés aux oiseaux, aux lapins et aux chevaux, qui peuvent subir des dommages cardiaques mortels. Chez le chien, la persine provoque une irritation gastro-intestinale légère — vomissements, diarrhée et douleurs abdominales. La préoccupation clinique majeure est le noyau, qui mesure 3-5 cm et peut provoquer une obstruction intestinale, particulièrement chez les chiens de moins de 20 kg. La teneur élevée en graisses de la chair (15-20 %) augmente également le risque de pancréatite chez les races prédisposées (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateAvocado.toxicityData.minimu: Faible toxicité de la chair — légers troubles gastro-intestinaux à toute quantité
emergency.ateAvocado.toxicityData.ld50: DL50 : La DL50 exacte de la persine est inconnue chez le chien ; l'obstruction par le noyau est la principale préoccupation clinique, pas la toxicité systémique
emergency.ateAvocado.toxicityData.source: Source : Centre antipoison animal ASPCA ; Buoro et al., 1994
emergency.ateAvocado.toxicityData.exampl: Exemple : Un chien de 10 kg mangeant de la chair d'avocat aura généralement des signes gastro-intestinaux légers ; un noyau avalé de 3-5 cm peut obstruer l'intestin grêle.
emergency.ateCaffeine.meta.title: Mon chien a mangé des pilules de caféine : guide d'urgence | petsMetrics
emergency.ateCaffeine.meta.description: Guide d'urgence : La caféine est toxique pour les chiens à partir de 140 mg/kg. Apprenez les symptômes (hyperactivité, arythmie, convulsions), l'évaluation des risques et les mesures immédiates. Centre antipoison ASPCA : (888) 426-4435.
emergency.ateCaffeine.meta.keywords: mon chien a mangé pilules caféine, toxicité caféine chiens, chien a mangé boisson énergisante, empoisonnement caféine chiens, que faire si chien mange caféine
emergency.ateCaffeine.banner.title: Mon chien a mangé des pilules de caféine : que faire maintenant
emergency.ateCaffeine.banner.subtitle: La caféine est une méthylxanthine toxique pour les chiens à partir de 140 mg/kg. Même 1-2 pilules (200 mg chacune) peuvent provoquer des convulsions chez les petits chiens. Appelez immédiatement le centre antipoison ASPCA au (888) 426-4435.
emergency.ateCaffeine.banner.cta: Trouver un vétérinaire d'urgence près de chez vous
emergency.ateCaffeine.article.headline: Mon chien a mangé des pilules de caféine : guide d'urgence
emergency.ateCaffeine.article.descriptio: Guide d'urgence pour la toxicité de la caféine chez le chien : symptômes, risque posologique et traitement.
emergency.ateCaffeine.article.ogTitle: Mon chien a mangé des pilules de caféine : guide d'urgence | petsMetrics
emergency.ateCaffeine.article.ogDescript: Que faire si votre chien mange des pilules de caféine.
emergency.ateCaffeine.science.content: La caféine (1,3,7-triméthylxanthine) est un antagoniste des récepteurs de l'adénosine et un inhibiteur de la phosphodiesterase. Chez le chien, elle provoque une stimulation du système nerveux central, une contraction des muscles cardiaques et une relaxation des muscles lisses. Les chiens métabolisent la caféine beaucoup plus lentement que les humains — la demi-vie chez le chien est de 4,5 heures contre 3 heures chez l'humain. Cela prolonge les effets toxiques. À fortes doses, la caféine provoque une libération excessive de catécholamines entraînant une tachycardie, une fibrillation et potentiellement la mort (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateCaffeine.toxicityData.minim: Symptômes légers à 20 mg/kg de poids corporel
emergency.ateCaffeine.toxicityData.examp: Exemple : 1-2 pilules de caféine (200 mg chacune) peuvent provoquer des symptômes graves chez un petit chien de moins de 10 kg.
emergency.ateAlcohol.meta.title: Mon chien a bu de l'alcool : guide d'urgence | petsMetrics
emergency.ateAlcohol.meta.description: Guide d'urgence : L'alcool est très toxique pour les chiens. Apprenez les symptômes (ataxie, dépression, acidose métabolique), le risque par type de boisson et les mesures immédiates. Centre antipoison ASPCA : (888) 426-4435.
emergency.ateAlcohol.meta.keywords: mon chien a bu alcool, toxicité alcool chiens, chien a bu bière, chien a mangé vin, empoisonnement éthanol chiens, alcool dangereux pour chiens
emergency.ateAlcohol.banner.title: Mon chien a bu de l'alcool : guide d'urgence
emergency.ateAlcohol.banner.subtitle: L'alcool (éthanol) est un dépresseur puissant du SNC chez le chien. Même de petites quantités provoquent une ataxie, une dépression et une acidose métabolique. Appelez immédiatement le centre antipoison ASPCA au (888) 426-4435.
emergency.ateAlcohol.banner.cta: Trouver un vétérinaire d'urgence près de chez vous
emergency.ateAlcohol.article.headline: Mon chien a bu de l'alcool : guide d'urgence
emergency.ateAlcohol.article.description: Guide d'urgence pour la toxicité de l'alcool chez le chien : symptômes, évaluation des risques et traitement.
emergency.ateAlcohol.article.ogTitle: Mon chien a bu de l'alcool : guide d'urgence | petsMetrics
emergency.ateAlcohol.article.ogDescripti: Que faire si votre chien boit de l'alcool.
emergency.ateAlcohol.science.content: L'éthanol (C2H5OH) est absorbé rapidement par le tractus gastro-intestinal et traverse la barrière hémato-encéphalique en quelques minutes. Les chiens manquent d'enzymes alcool déshydrogénase efficaces, les rendant 3 à 5 fois plus sensibles que les humains. L'éthanol inhibe les récepteurs NMDA et renforce l'activité GABA, provoquant une dépression du SNC, une dépression respiratoire et une acidose métabolique. La dose létale chez le chien est de 5,5 mL/kg d'éthanol pur. La pâte à pain crue est doublement dangereuse — la fermentation des levures continue dans l'estomac chaud, produisant plus d'alcool et faisant gonfler la pâte (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateAlcohol.toxicityData.minimu: Aussi peu que 1,5 mL/kg d'éthanol pur peut provoquer une intoxication notable
emergency.ateAlcohol.toxicityData.source: Source : Manuel vétérinaire Merck ; Centre antipoison animal ASPCA
emergency.ateAlcohol.toxicityData.exampl: Exemple : Une seule bière de 355 ml (5 % d'alcool = 17 g d'éthanol) peut provoquer une intoxication sévère chez un petit chien de moins de 10 kg.

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.meta.descript: Guide d'urgence : Les noix de macadamia sont toxiques pour les chiens. Apprenez les symptômes (faiblesse, vomissements, tremblements), l'évaluation des risques selon le poids du chien et les mesures immédiates. Centre antipoison ASPCA : (888) 426-4435.

Appelez le centre antipoison ASPCA au (888) 426-4435 pour des conseils immédiats.

emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.article.ogTit: Mon chien a mangé des noix de macadamia : guide d'urgence | petsMetrics
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.article.ogDes: Que faire si votre chien mange des noix de macadamia.
emergency.ateMacadamiaNuts.science.conte: Les noix de macadamia contiennent une toxine non identifiée qui affecte de manière unique le système neuromusculaire des chiens. Le composé provoque une faiblesse réversible et une ataxie des membres postérieurs, probablement par perturbation de la signalisation des neurones moteurs. Contrairement à de nombreuses toxines, le mécanisme exact reste inconnu malgré des décennies d'observation clinique. La recherche de Morton (2002) a établi la DL50 à 2,4 g/kg. La toxine est thermostable et présente sous toutes les formes : crues, grillées, salées et dans les produits de boulangerie. Les symptômes sont dose-dépendants et se résolvent généralement en 12 à 48 heures avec des soins de soutien (ASPCA, 2023).
Dose toxique minimale : 0,5 g/kg de poids corporel (symptômes légers)
DL50 : 2,4 g/kg de poids corporel (symptômes graves)
Source : Morton, 2002 — Journal of Veterinary Diagnostic Investigation
Exemple : Un chien de 15 kg (33 lb) mangeant 15 g de noix de macadamia (environ 12-15 noix) atteindrait le seuil toxique minimal. Une noix typique pèse environ 1,2 à 1,5 g.

emergency.ateMushrooms.meta.description: Guide d'urgence : Les champignons sauvages peuvent être mortellement toxiques pour les chiens. Apprenez sur l'empoisonnement par Amanita (insuffisance hépatique), le délai d'apparition des symptômes et pourquoi chaque ingestion de champignon est une urgence. Centre antipoison ASPCA : (888) 426-4435.

emergency.ateMushrooms.article.headline: Mon chien a mangé un champignon dans le jardin : guide d'urgence
emergency.ateMushrooms.article.descripti: Guide d'urgence pour la toxicité des champignons sauvages chez le chien : empoisonnement par Amanita, risque d'insuffisance hépatique et traitement immédiat.
emergency.ateMushrooms.article.ogTitle: Mon chien a mangé un champignon : guide d'urgence | petsMetrics
emergency.ateMushrooms.article.ogDescrip: Guide d'urgence : Les champignons sauvages peuvent provoquer une insuffisance hépatique mortelle chez les chiens. Agissez immédiatement.
emergency.ateMushrooms.banner.title: Mon chien a mangé un champignon dans le jardin : que faire maintenant
emergency.ateMushrooms.banner.subtitle: Les champignons sauvages peuvent provoquer une insuffisance hépatique mortelle — les symptômes sont RETARDÉS de 6 à 24 heures. N'attendez pas les symptômes. Appelez immédiatement le centre antipoison ASPCA au (888) 426-4435.
emergency.ateMushrooms.science.content: Les amatoxines (alpha-amanitine, beta-amanitine) sont des octapeptides bicycliques présents dans les espèces Amanita, Galerina et Lepiota. Elles inhibent l'ARN polymérase II, stoppant la synthèse protéique dans les hépatocytes. Le foie est la cible principale car les amatoxines subissent une recirculation entérohépatique. Après ingestion, il y a une période de latence de 6 à 12 heures, suivie d'une phase de gastro-entérite, une brève fausse récupération (12 à 24 heures), puis une insuffisance hépatique fulminante avec coagulopathie, encéphalopathie et décès. Le traitement dans les 12 heures a un taux de survie de 90 % ; après 24 heures, la survie chute à 30 % (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateMushrooms.toxicityData.mini: 0,1 mg/kg d'amatoxine (un bonnet de la mort = 10-15 mg)
emergency.ateMushrooms.toxicityData.ld50: Non bien établi ; 0,1 mg/kg d'amatoxine potentiellement mortel
emergency.ateMushrooms.toxicityData.exam: Un seul chapeau d'Amanita phalloides contient assez d'amatoxine pour tuer un chien de 10-20 kg. L'ingestion partielle reste mortelle.
emergency.ateCookedBones.meta.title: Mon chien a mangé des os cuits : guide d'urgence | petsMetrics
emergency.ateCookedBones.meta.descriptio: Guide d'urgence : Les os cuits se fragmentent et peuvent provoquer une perforation ou occlusion intestinale. Apprenez les symptômes (vomissements, selles sanglantes, douleur), quand appeler le vétérinaire et les conseils de prévention.
emergency.ateCookedBones.meta.keywords: mon chien a mangé os cuits, danger os cuits chiens, chien a mangé os poulet, os fragmenté chien, os cuits mauvais pour chiens
emergency.ateCookedBones.article.headlin: Mon chien a mangé des os cuits : guide d'urgence
emergency.ateCookedBones.article.descrip: Guide d'urgence pour l'ingestion d'os cuits chez le chien : risque d'éclats, occlusion et traitement.
emergency.ateCookedBones.article.ogTitle: Mon chien a mangé des os cuits : guide d'urgence | petsMetrics
emergency.ateCookedBones.article.ogDescr: Guide d'urgence : Les os cuits peuvent se fragmenter et provoquer des dommages intestinaux mortels.
emergency.ateCookedBones.banner.title: Mon chien a mangé des os cuits : que faire maintenant
emergency.ateCookedBones.banner.subtitle: Les os cuits se fragmentent en morceaux tranchants qui peuvent percer la paroi intestinale ou provoquer une occlusion mortelle. Il s'agit d'une urgence mécanique, pas d'un empoisonnement. Appelez immédiatement votre vétérinaire.
emergency.ateCookedBones.science.content: La cuisson dénature le collagène dans les os, les rendant cassants et sujets à la fragmentation. Les os crus contiennent du collagène flexible et sont moins susceptibles de se fragmenter. Lorsque les os cuits se fragmentent, les morceaux tranchants (ostéoïdes) peuvent percer la paroi gastro-intestinale, provoquant une péritonite — une infection mortelle. Les sites de perforation les plus courants sont l'œsophage (si avalé incorrectement), l'estomac et la jonction iléocæcale (où l'intestin grêle se rétrécit). Les os de volaille sont particulièrement dangereux car ils sont creux et se brisent en éclats aiguës comme des aiguilles (AAHA, 2023).
emergency.ateCookedBones.toxicityData.mi: N/A (risque mécanique — tout fragment de taille peut causer des dommages)
emergency.ateCookedBones.toxicityData.ld: Non applicable — traumatisme physique, pas toxicité chimique
emergency.ateCookedBones.toxicityData.so: Lignes directrices AAHA, Manuel vétérinaire Merck
emergency.ateCookedBones.toxicityData.ex: Un seul os de poulet peut se briser en dizaines d'éclats aiguës comme des aiguilles qui agissent comme de petits couteaux dans le tractus gastro-intestinal.

emergency.atePlastic.meta.description: Emergency guide: Plastic can cause intestinal blockage in dogs. Learn symptoms (vomiting, no bowel movement), size-based risk assessment, and when emergency surgery is needed. ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435.

emergency.atePlastic.article.headline: My Dog Ate Plastic: What to Do Now
emergency.atePlastic.article.description: Emergency guide for plastic ingestion in dogs: obstruction risk, symptoms, and treatment options.
emergency.atePlastic.article.ogTitle: My Dog Ate Plastic: What to Do Now | petsMetrics
emergency.atePlastic.article.ogDescripti: Emergency guide: Plastic can cause life-threatening intestinal blockage in dogs.
emergency.atePlastic.banner.severityLabe: MONITOR — Obstruction Risk Depends on Size
emergency.atePlastic.banner.title: My Dog Ate Plastic: What to Do Now
emergency.atePlastic.banner.subtitle: Plastic is non-toxic but can cause dangerous intestinal blockage. Risk depends on the size and shape of the object. Call your vet if the piece is larger than 2cm.
emergency.atePlastic.decisionGuide.safe: Plastic piece smaller than 2cm (e.g., corner of wrapper). Monitor stool for 48 hours.
emergency.atePlastic.decisionGuide.call: Plastic piece 2-3cm OR your dog shows ANY vomiting/lethargy. X-ray may be needed.
emergency.atePlastic.decisionGuide.emerg: Plastic larger than 3cm, OR persistent vomiting, OR no bowel movement in 48 hours. Surgery likely needed.
emergency.atePlastic.science.content: Plastic is chemically inert and non-toxic to dogs — the danger is purely mechanical. The canine GI tract narrows at two critical points: the pylorus (stomach exit, ~1-2cm diameter in small dogs) and the ileocecal junction (small-to-large intestine transition). Objects wider than these passages become lodged, causing a complete or partial obstruction. Complete obstructions cause fluid accumulation, electrolyte imbalances, and intestinal necrosis within 48-72 hours. Surgical intervention is required for objects that do not pass within 24-48 hours or cause persistent vomiting (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).
emergency.atePlastic.toxicityData.exampl: A 2cm plastic toy ball will not pass through a medium-sized dog's pylorus. Objects >2cm require vet assessment.

emergency.ateMedication.meta.description: Emergency guide: Human medications are toxic to dogs. Learn about ibuprofen (NSAID), acetaminophen, and antidepressant toxicity risks, symptoms, and immediate actions. ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435.

emergency.ateMedication.article.ogTitle: My Dog Ate Human Medication: Emergency Guide | petsMetrics
emergency.ateMedication.article.ogDescri: Emergency guide: Human medications like ibuprofen are toxic to dogs. Act immediately.
emergency.ateMedication.banner.severityL: TOXIC — Human Medication Can Be Fatal to Dogs
emergency.ateMedication.banner.title: My Dog Ate Human Medication: What to Do Now
emergency.ateMedication.banner.subtitle: Human medications are a leading cause of pet poisoning. Even one pill of ibuprofen or acetaminophen can kill a dog. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 IMMEDIATELY.
emergency.ateMedication.science.content: Dogs metabolize many drugs differently than humans. NSAIDs (ibuprofen) inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, reducing protective prostaglandins in the GI tract and kidneys, leading to ulceration and renal failure. Acetaminophen depletes glutathione in canine hepatocytes and converts hemoglobin to methemoglobin, impairing oxygen transport. Dogs are particularly sensitive to many ADHD medications (amphetamines) due to their effect on catecholamine release. Even "harmless" supplements like vitamin D can cause fatal hypercalcemia when ingested in large amounts (ASPCA, 2023).
emergency.ateMedication.toxicityData.min: Drug-dependent: Ibuprofen 50mg/kg, Acetaminophen 75mg/kg, single pill of some ADHD meds
emergency.ateMedication.toxicityData.exa: A single 200mg ibuprofen tablet can cause kidney failure in a 4kg dog. Five tablets (1000mg) = 250mg/kg = potentially fatal dose.

emergency.ateRodenticide.meta.descriptio: Emergency guide: Rodenticide (rat poison) is extremely toxic to dogs. Learn about anticoagulant vs neurotoxic types, symptoms, and why immediate treatment is critical. ASPCA Poison Control: (888) 426-4435.

emergency.ateRodenticide.article.ogTitle: My Dog Ate Rat Poison: Emergency Guide | petsMetrics
emergency.ateRodenticide.article.ogDescr: Emergency guide: Rodenticide is deadly toxic to dogs. Even small amounts require immediate treatment.
emergency.ateRodenticide.banner.title: My Dog Ate Rat Poison: What to Do Now
emergency.ateRodenticide.banner.subtitle: Rodenticide is one of the deadliest dog toxins. Do not wait for symptoms — anticoagulant effects are delayed 2-5 days. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 and go to emergency vet NOW.
emergency.ateRodenticide.science.content: Anticoagulant rodenticides inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), preventing recycling of vitamin K. This depletes active clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X), causing spontaneous hemorrhage. Second-generation anticoagulants (brodifacoum, bromadiolone) are 100x more potent than warfarin and persist in the liver for weeks. Bromethalin uncouples oxidative phosphorylation in brain cells, causing cerebral edema and increased intracranial pressure. Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) causes hypercalcemia, leading to metastatic calcification of kidneys, heart, and blood vessels (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateTobacco.riskAssessment.head: Nicotine Source
Risk Level
emergency.ateTobacco.science.content: Nicotine is an alkaloid that binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) in the autonomic ganglia, neuromuscular junctions, and CNS. At low doses, it stimulates receptors causing tachycardia, hypertension, and CNS excitation. At high doses, it causes receptor depolarization blockade, leading to bradycardia, respiratory paralysis, and coma. The biphasic effect (stimulation then depression) is pathognomonic. Dogs metabolize nicotine primarily via hepatic N-oxidation, with a half-life of approximately 1.5 hours. E-liquid poses extreme danger because 1mL can contain 3-24mg of nicotine absorbed rapidly through oral mucosa (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateMarijuana.banner.subtitle: Dogs are more sensitive to THC than humans. Edibles (gummies, brownies) are especially dangerous due to high concentration. Call ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435.
emergency.ateMarijuana.honestySection.ti: 📋 Important: Be Honest With Your Vet
emergency.ateMarijuana.honestySection.co: Veterinarians are required to treat, not report, pet poisonings. Accurate information about marijuana ingestion ensures your dog receives proper care without unnecessary testing. Your honesty is protected and helps save your dog's life.
emergency.ateMarijuana.science.content: Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) binds to CB1 cannabinoid receptors in the canine central nervous system. Dogs have a higher density of CB1 receptors in the cerebellum (responsible for coordination) and brainstem than humans, explaining their heightened sensitivity. THC is lipophilic and undergoes enterohepatic recirculation, prolonging effects. Edibles are dangerous because the GI tract absorbs THC rapidly, and the liver converts 11-hydroxy-THC, which is 5x more psychoactive. Most cases are supportive — there is no specific antidote, but IV lipid emulsion therapy can accelerate THC clearance (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateXylitolGum.science.content: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol (polyol) that triggers a rapid, exaggerated insulin release from canine beta cells — up to 6-7x the amount released by glucose. This is because dogs metabolize xylitol via the same pathway as glucose but with different kinetics. The resulting hypoglycemia (blood glucose <60mg/dL) causes neurological dysfunction, seizures, and death. At higher doses (>0.5g/kg), xylitol causes acute hepatic necrosis through ATP depletion and oxidative stress. The mechanism is dose-dependent and unique to dogs — cats appear to be less susceptible (ASPCA, 2023).

While humans eliminate theobromine in 2-3 hours, dogs take 17.5 hours or more. This allows toxic levels to build up in their system. Theobromine affects the central nervous system, cardiovascular system, and smooth muscles. At high doses, it causes seizures, cardiac arrhythmias, and potentially death (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateOnion.science.content: Onions contain thiosulfate compounds (n-propyl disulfide) that dogs cannot metabolize. These compounds cause oxidative damage to red blood cells, forming Heinz bodies — damaged hemoglobin that precipitates inside the cell. The spleen then destroys these damaged cells, leading to hemolytic anemia. This process takes 1-3 days, which is why symptoms are delayed (ASPCA, 2023).

emergency.ateSock.science.content: Fabric foreign bodies are particularly dangerous because they can become lodged at the pyloric sphincter (stomach exit) or in the small intestine. Once stuck, they cause a complete blockage — nothing can pass, and the intestinal wall may become necrotic (die) from pressure. This leads to perforation, peritonitis, and death without surgical intervention. Puppies and small dogs are at highest risk due to their narrower intestinal diameter (AVMA, 2023).

emergency.ateAntifreeze.science.content: Ethylene glycol itself is not toxic — it is the metabolites produced by the liver that cause damage. Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethylene glycol to glycoaldehyde, then glycolic acid, then oxalic acid. Oxalic acid binds with calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals that destroy kidney tissue. This process causes metabolic acidosis and acute kidney failure within 12-36 hours. The antidote works by blocking alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing toxic metabolite formation (ASPCA, 2023).

Cytochrome P450 enzymes in feline liver have reduced activity compared to dogs, causing prolonged theobromine half-life. This leads to cumulative effects on the CNS (seizures), cardiovascular system (arrhythmias), and smooth muscles. Cats are also obligate carnivores with less capacity to process plant-derived alkaloids. The combination of smaller body weight, slower metabolism, and greater sensitivity makes chocolate proportionally more dangerous for cats (ASPCA, 2023).

catEmergency.ateOnion.science.content: Onions (Allium cepa) contain N-propyl disulfide and S-methylcysteine sulfoxide. These compounds cause oxidative damage to hemoglobin, forming Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin precipitates). The spleen removes damaged cells, causing hemolytic anemia. Cats are especially vulnerable because feline hemoglobin contains more sulfhydryl groups than other species, making it more susceptible to oxidation. Additionally, cats have lower glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) activity, reducing their ability to protect red blood cells from oxidative injury. Anemia typically peaks 3-5 days post-ingestion (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).

catEmergency.ateGarlic.science.content: Garlic (Allium sativum) contains alliin, which converts to allicin when crushed or chewed. Allicin and its derivatives (allyl propyl disulfide, ajoene) cause oxidative denaturation of hemoglobin in feline erythrocytes. The feline hemoglobin molecule has 8-10 sulfhydryl groups (vs 2-4 in dogs), making it 2-3x more susceptible to oxidative damage. The resulting Heinz bodies are phagocytosed by splenic macrophages, causing extravascular hemolysis. Unlike onions, garlic's thiosulfates are more bioavailable in cats due to differences in hepatic metabolism (Merck Veterinary Manual, 2023).

catEmergency.ateEssentialOils.science.co: Cats lack UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A6 and UGT1A9) enzymes required for phase II glucuronidation of terpenes (d-limonene, alpha-terpineol) and phenols (eugenol, thymol). These compounds accumulate in the hepatobiliary system, causing hepatotoxicity and neurotoxicity. Cats also have deficient P-glycoprotein efflux transporters at the blood-brain barrier, increasing CNS exposure. Tea tree oil (Melaleuca alternifolia) monoterpenes cause dose-dependent CNS depression, ataxia, and hypothermia. Even 10mL applied dermally can be fatal in cats (ASPCA, 2023).

catEmergency.ateFishingLine.science.cont: Linear foreign bodies (string, yarn, fishing line) are surgical emergencies in cats. The proximal end anchors — commonly under the tongue, at the pylorus, or in the stomach. Intestinal peristalsis pulls the distal end taught, causing the intestine to plicate (accordion-fold) around it. The taut line exerts pressure on the mesenteric border, causing ischemic necrosis and perforation. Multiple perforations along the intestinal tract lead to septic peritonitis. Unlike dogs, cats have a smaller intestinal diameter and are more susceptible to linear foreign body complications (AAHA, 2023).

catEmergency.ateLily.science.content: The exact toxic compound in lilies is unidentified, but it causes acute tubular necrosis in feline kidneys. Cats are uniquely susceptible — dogs and humans can eat lilies without harm. The toxin is water-soluble and present in all plant parts: petals, leaves, stems, pollen, and even vase water. Kidney damage begins within hours and progresses to complete renal failure within 24-72 hours without treatment. Early IV fluid therapy (within 18 hours) can prevent permanent damage (ASPCA, 2023).

This causes the intestines to bunch up ("pleat") along the string, and the taut string can saw through the intestinal wall like a wire. This leads to perforation, peritonitis, sepsis, and death without surgical intervention. Cats are especially prone due to their barbed tongues that easily catch string (AAFP, 2023).
compare.breedMatters: Breed matters. Golden Retrievers, German Shepherds, and Boxers have different cancer risk profiles than small breeds. Discuss your specific breed's risk factors with your veterinarian before deciding on timing.
compare.dryVsWet.title: Dry Food vs Wet Food for Dogs: Which Is Right?
compare.dryVsWet.subtitle: A science-based comparison of kibble and canned diets — covering cost, dental health, shelf life, hydration, and palatability. No marketing fluff, just data from AAFCO and veterinary nutritionists.
compare.dryVsWet.topicA.bestFor: Active adult dogs, large breeds, multi-dog households on a budget, and owners who value convenience.
compare.dryVsWet.topicB.bestFor: Senior dogs, small breeds, picky eaters, dogs with dental issues, kidney/urinary conditions, and dogs who don't drink enough water.
compare.dryVsWet.verdict: Most dogs do well on a mixed feeding approach. A base of quality kibble for cost-efficiency and dental crunch, supplemented with a small amount of wet food for hydration and palatability. For dogs with kidney disease, urinary issues, or senior dogs with appetite loss, increase wet food proportion. For active large-breed adults on a budget, kibble as the primary diet is perfectly adequate. Consult your veterinarian if your dog has specific health conditions.
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.subtitle: Data-driven comparison of indoor-only and outdoor-access cats — covering lifespan, disease risk, injury rates, behavioral needs, and the "best of both worlds" middle ground. Based on AAFP and ISFM feline welfare guidelines.
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicA.bestFor: Most urban/suburban cat owners who can provide adequate environmental enrichment.
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.topicB.bestFor: Rural properties with controlled outdoor access (catio, enclosed garden) and owners who accept the risks.
compare.indoorVsOutdoor.verdict: The safest and most recommended approach is "Indoor + Enrichment" or "Supervised Outdoor Access." An indoor-only cat with proper environmental enrichment (cat trees, window perches, puzzle feeders, daily interactive play) lives significantly longer and healthier than a free-roaming outdoor cat. If you want your cat to experience the outdoors, consider a catio (enclosed outdoor pen), a secure garden with cat-proof fencing, or leash walks with a harness. This provides outdoor stimulation while maintaining the safety and longevity benefits of indoor living.
compare.rawVsKibble.title: Raw Diet vs Kibble for Dogs: Science, Safety & Cost Compared
compare.rawVsKibble.subtitle: An objective comparison of BARF (Biologically Appropriate Raw Food) diets and commercial kibble — covering nutritional completeness, bacterial risks, dental benefits, and practical feasibility. Based on AVMA, NRC, and peer-reviewed research.
compare.rawVsKibble.topicA.bestFor: Dedicated owners with veterinary nutritionist guidance, dogs with specific food intolerances not resolved by commercial diets, and those willing to invest significant time and resources.
compare.rawVsKibble.topicB.bestFor: The vast majority of dog owners — especially those without access to a board-certified veterinary nutritionist or the budget/time for raw feeding.
compare.rawVsKibble.verdict: For most dog owners, a high-quality commercial kibble is the safest, most practical choice. If you are committed to raw feeding, work with a board-certified veterinary nutritionist (ACVN) to ensure nutritional completeness, follow strict hygiene protocols, and understand the 30% bacterial contamination risk. The dental benefits of raw bones can be achieved safely with professional dental cleaning and appropriate chew toys. A middle-ground approach — high-quality kibble supplemented with raw meaty bones as treats (not meals) — captures some benefits while minimizing risks.
compare.spayedVsUnspayed.title: Spayed vs Unspayed Dog: Health, Behavior & Timing
compare.spayedVsUnspayed.subtitle: A balanced comparison of spay/neuter vs. keeping your dog intact — covering cancer risks, orthopedic concerns, behavioral changes, and breed-specific timing recommendations. Based on AAHA and AVMA veterinary guidelines.
compare.spayedVsUnspayed.topicA.bestFor: Most dogs, especially small breeds, mixed breeds, and any dog not intended for responsible breeding programs.
compare.spayedVsUnspayed.topicB.bestFor: Large/giant breeds where delayed spay/neuter benefits joint health (discuss timing with vet), responsibly managed breeding programs, and dogs where cancer risk from spaying is a particular breed concern.
compare.spayedVsUnspayed.verdict: The benefits of spaying/neutering outweigh the risks for most dogs. For small breeds (<20kg), spay/neuter at 6–12 months is well-supported. For large breeds (25–45kg), consider delaying to 12–18 months to protect joint development. For giant breeds (>45kg), some veterinarians recommend 18–24 months. Discuss your specific breed's cancer and joint health risks with your veterinarian to determine the optimal timing. Never skip the conversation — the "when" matters as much as the "whether."
